rationale: The IBS-IBD continuum concept provides biological rationale for why no single diagnostic reference standard exists for IBD.
The continuum concept challenges the discrete diagnostic categories that ileocolonoscopy aims to establish between CD and UC.
The difficulty defining disease severity for trial populations parallels the absence of a single diagnostic reference standard.
The AGA 2021 GRADE approach with formal network meta-analysis represents methodological advancement over the non-GRADE-rated ACG 2018 statements.
The finding that corticosteroids fail to consistently achieve mucosal healing reinforces mucosal healing as the true therapeutic goal.
The bridge-not-destination framing of corticosteroids supports mucosal healing as the genuine treatment endpoint.
Anti-TNF agents achieve mucosal healing, operationalizing the abstract therapeutic goal with a concrete class of agents.
The ACG CD negative recommendation limits 5-ASA efficacy to UC only, clarifying the disease-specific scope of the ECCO UC induction claim.
The ACG UC claim refines the general oral 5-ASA induction claim by specifying proctitis first-line therapy and combination superiority.
The ECCO maintenance recommendation extends the ACG induction and location-specific claims into the maintenance setting.
Both ACG and ECCO independently conclude that corticosteroids provide symptomatic relief without reliably achieving mucosal healing.
The budesonide MMX recommendation for 5-ASA-refractory patients logically presupposes 5-ASA first-line therapy has been attempted.
The ECCO guideline operationalizes the AGA thiopurine maintenance evidence by specifying steroid-dependent and 5-ASA-intolerant patient populations.
The ACG CD negative recommendation and ACG UC positive recommendation together reveal that 5-ASA maintenance efficacy is disease-specific.
ECCO CD confirms 5-ASA is ineffective for CD maintenance while ACG UC affirms efficacy for UC, establishing a clear disease-divergent efficacy pattern.
Near-identical recommendations from ECCO and ACG agree that the inducing agent should be continued and that 5-ASA has no post-advanced-therapy maintenance role.
The ECCO claim restricts the ACG general 5-ASA maintenance assertion by specifying that 5-ASA has no role after advanced therapy initiation.
The AGA CD 2021 guideline independently confirms the ACG CD 2018 finding that 5-ASA and corticosteroids lack maintenance efficacy.
ECCO and AGA guidelines converge on the same conclusion: 5-ASA is ineffective for CD maintenance across multiple evidence reviews.
Both ECCO and AGA independently recommend against 5-ASA and sulfasalazine for inducing remission in CD.
The ECCO topical 5-ASA superiority finding extends the ACG general maintenance claim by specifying the comparative advantage over topical steroids.
ACG UC and AGA CD independently agree that corticosteroids have no maintenance role, reinforcing this principle across both diseases.
ECCO sharpens the AGA claim from infliximab having the best evidence to being the only biologic with RCT-level fistula healing evidence.
The ACG ustekinumab efficacy data across biologic-naive and anti-TNF-failure populations provides the evidence base for AGA's preference recommendation.
The ACG ustekinumab efficacy evidence directly supports the AGA strong recommendation for ustekinumab over no treatment.
ECCO's meta-analytic evidence for ustekinumab and vedolizumab induction efficacy supports AGA's strong recommendation for these biologics.
The CD guideline restricts the UC guideline's broad combination therapy principle to the best-evidenced biologic, infliximab, with lower certainty for adalimumab.
ECCO extends the ACG ustekinumab efficacy claim by adding vedolizumab and specifying efficacy across both biologic-naive and anti-TNF-experienced populations.
The ACG maintenance claim for vedolizumab and ustekinumab logically depends on the ECCO evidence that these agents are effective for induction.
